newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Cuba says health services badly hit by hurricane.
newsitem.headline: Cuba says health services badly hit by hurricane.

text.p: Cuba has reported that its health services, the pride of its communist system, have been severely hit by Hurricane Lili which swept across the country last week, the United Nations said on Friday.
The Cuban Health Ministry estimated the cost alone of replacing medicines and medical supplies destroyed at around $5.7 million, the world body's Department of Humanitarian Affairs (DHA) said.

Relaying an appeal for international assistance from the island, DHA cited the ministry as saying 21 hospitals and dozens of clinics had been damaged, and the water supply throughout the country had been contaminated.

A quarter of the beds in three main hospitals had been lost and two others had to be totally evacuated as a result of the hurricane, which also wrecked 5,000 homes, cut communications lines and destroyed crops in central and western areas of Cuba.
The ministry also reported that six old people's homes had been damaged and eight warehouses full of pharmaceutical supplies had been totally destroyed.
Cuba, supported by U.N. and other international surveys, has long argued that its largely free health services are the best and most comprehensive in Latin America.

But the health system was badly bit by the economic crisis which followed the collapse in 1991 of the Soviet Union, the island's main trading partner, and the subsequent withdrawal of support by Moscow and east European countries.

The DHA report followed a controversy over hurricane relief aid to Cuba from the United States, where some Cuban Americans have mobilised to send help but are opposed by others who argue it would help prop up the rule of President Fidel Castro.

U.S. authorities have waived a ban on direct flights to the island -- under a Washington economic embargo for four decades -- to allow the Roman Catholic charity Caritas Cubana to send a planeload of food.

But a Cuban Foreign Ministry official said on Thursday no political strings should be attached to the aid, and a Caritas official said the Havana authorities had made clear packages could not be stamped with political slogans.

The DHA report issued in Geneva said the Cuban Health Ministry was stepping up its disease-prevention programme in the wake of Hurricane Lili and was especially watching for any upsurge in intestinal infections and pneumonia.
The first priority for assistance was water purification equipment or funds to buy it, pesticides and spraying equipment essential medicines and rehabilitation of main hospitals.
DHA said Spain had already sent a relief flight with food, construction material and medical supplies worth $195,000.
Reports from Havana said Mexico, which was the first to respond to the Cuban appeal earlier this week, sent two planeloads of food and roofing material.

DHA, which said it was ready to serve as a channel for cash contributions to be used during the immediate relief phase, said it would provide donor governments with written confirmation of how the funds were used.
